steps.explain: Rotating a complex number anticlockwise by \(\theta\) without changing its length means multiplying by \(\operatorname{cis}\theta\).

parts.answer: ABCD is a parallelogram, so AD ∥ BC and co-interior angles give \(\angle DCB=\pi-\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{\pi}{3}\). Also \(|d-c|=|b-c|\), i.e. CD = CB. So \(\overrightarrow{CD}\) is \(\overrightarrow{CB}\) rotated anticlockwise by \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) with the same length: \(d-c=(b-c)\operatorname{cis}\frac{\pi}{3}=(b-c)\left(\frac12+\frac{i\sqrt3}{2}\right)\).

keyPoints.note: ∠DCB = π − 2π/3 = π/3 and CD = CB, so CD is CB rotated anticlockwise by π/3.

parts.hint: arg((a − d)/(b − d)) is the angle from DB to DA. The figure is a rhombus.

steps.explain: \(\arg\left(\frac{a-d}{b-d}\right)=\arg(a-d)-\arg(b-d)\): the angle turned anticlockwise from \(\overrightarrow{DB}\) to \(\overrightarrow{DA}\), i.e. \(\angle BDA\).
A parallelogram with a pair of equal adjacent sides (\(CD=CB\)) is a rhombus, and the diagonals of a rhombus bisect its angles. So \(DB\) bisects \(\angle ADC=\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

steps.explain: From the diagram, \(e^{i\theta}\) is in the second quadrant, a little past the imaginary axis: \(\frac\pi2\lt\theta\lt\pi\). All the options have modulus 1, so only the argument matters.
\(e^{-i\theta}\) has argument \(-\theta\): it is the reflection of \(e^{i\theta}\) in the real axis, so it lands in the third quadrant.
Multiplying by \(i\) rotates a point \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise (adds \(\frac\pi2\) to the argument).

Since \(\frac\pi2\lt\theta\lt\pi\), the new argument is between \(-\frac\pi2\) and 0: the fourth quadrant, close to the positive real axis (because \(\theta\) is only a little more than \(\frac\pi2\)).

In an Argand diagram \(z\) is a point on the circle \(|z|=2\).

Given that \(\arg z=\theta\) and \(0 \lt \theta \lt \frac{\pi}{2}\).

parts.stem: Draw a diagram to represent this information.
parts.hint: |z| = 2 is a circle of radius 2 about O; 0 < θ < π/2 is the first quadrant.

steps.explain: \(|z|=2\) means \(z\) is 2 units from the origin, so \(z\) lies on the circle centred at \(O\) with radius 2. It crosses the axes at \(\pm2\) and \(\pm2i\).
\(0 \lt \arg z \lt \frac\pi2\) puts \(z\) in the first quadrant. Draw \(Oz\) and mark \(\theta\) between the positive real axis and \(Oz\).

keyPoints.note: Draw the circle of radius 2 about O and put z in the first quadrant with angle θ from the positive real axis.

parts.stem: Find, in terms of \(\theta\), an expression for \(\arg z^2\).
parts.hint: arg(z²) = 2 arg z.

steps.explain: Write \(z\) in modulus-argument form.
By de Moivre's theorem the modulus is squared and the argument is doubled.
Since \(0 \lt \theta \lt \frac\pi2\), we have \(0 \lt 2\theta \lt \pi\), which is already a principal argument.

keyPoints.note: Multiplying complex numbers adds arguments, so arg(z²) = 2 arg z.

parts.stem:
Find, in terms of \(\theta\), giving brief reasons, an expression for:

(A) \(\arg(z+2)\)
parts.hint: z + 2 is the diagonal of a rhombus with sides z and 2.

steps.explain: Add \(z\) and \(2\) as vectors: they are adjacent sides of a parallelogram with vertices \(O\), \(2\), \(z+2\), \(z\).
In a rhombus the diagonal bisects the angle between the sides. The sides from \(O\) make angles \(0\) and \(\theta\) with the real axis.
